    Yes. You’re thinking of the parable of the blind men and the elephant, an ancient story found in several traditions, especially associated with Jain, Buddhist, and Hindu literature.

    The basic metaphor is:

    • One blind man touches the trunk and says the elephant is like a snake.
    • Another touches the leg and says it is like a tree.
    • Another touches the ear and says it is like a fan.
    • Another touches the side and says it is like a wall.
    • Another touches the tusk and says it is like a spear.
    • Each person is accurately describing the part they can perceive, yet they reach an erroneous conclusion about the whole.

    The interesting philosophical point is that the men aren't necessarily wrong about their observations. They're wrong when they mistake a partial observation for the complete nature of the thing.

    That makes it a particularly fertile metaphor for an axiom. We could potentially distill it into something like:

    A partial truth becomes a falsehood when it claims to be the whole truth.

    Or, more neutrally:

    No perspective upon a complex whole is equivalent to the whole itself.

    If you'd like, we can brainstorm this together and keep tightening the metaphor until we arrive at an axiom that feels genuinely yours.
